questions.stem: A mail assistant reads inbound messages. Which combination gives the best protection against a hostile message?

options.text: A pattern list, a firm tone in the prompt and a larger context window
options.says: Ruled out because a pattern list "catches the phrasing someone thought of and misses the paraphrase", and "Whatever the injected text asks for, the agent can do only what its grants allow", so tone adds no grant.

options.text: Encoded results, narrow tools and a gate that tightens after outside text
options.says: The layers table puts structure (JSON encoding), privilege (narrow tools, "a stricter gate after untrusted text was read") and a decision gate in the path of one request.

options.text: Encoded results, a pattern list and broad tools kept for convenience
options.says: Ruled out because "An agent that can read a file, send mail to anyone and has the production key can leak."

options.text: Narrow tools and a gate, with the message text placed in the system prompt
options.says: Ruled out because the page says untrusted content goes "never in `system` prompts or plain user `text` blocks".

questions.stem: After an agent has read an untrusted web page, which request should be refused or escalated?

options.text: Reading a file inside the project folder
options.says: Ruled out because "Reads stay allowed, since they change nothing".

options.text: Fetching a plain address with no query string and no fragment
options.says: Ruled out because only a network call "that carries data in its URL, a query string or a fragment asks", so a plain address stays allowed.

options.text: Sending mail to an outside recipient
options.says: The page says that in a tainted session "Sending mail is refused until a person does it".

options.text: Running a read-only command such as `git status`
options.says: Ruled out because the practice gate "limits `bash` to read-only commands and refuses chaining", so a read-only command stays allowed.

origin.section: A session that has read untrusted text

questions.stem: A team builds a hook to stop recursive forced deletes. Which design choice should the hook follow?

options.text: Parse the line into parts, fail closed, and stay silent on safe ones
options.says: The page says a hook can "parse the command into its parts", should "fail closed", and that a command "that cannot be parsed, or an event the hook cannot read, is blocked and not waved through".

options.text: Match the text `rm -rf` and allow whatever it cannot parse
options.says: Ruled out because "A guard that exits 0 on a parse error is a guard an attacker can walk through".

options.text: Match the text `rm -rf` and rely on the model's caution for the rest
options.says: Ruled out because "A memory line asks, and a hook enforces", and the model's caution is not a control.

options.text: Answer `allow` on every safe command so the call goes straight through
options.says: Ruled out because the hook "should answer the safe case with no opinion and not with an allow, so that it never overrides a stricter rule elsewhere".

questions.stem: A team's key is stored in the environment for a CI job. Which practice fits both CI and an agent in production?

options.text: Track the `.env` file so every runner receives the same value
options.says: Ruled out because keys are "loaded from an untracked file such as `.env`", and a secret never enters "a file anyone can commit".

options.text: Pass it to the agent's sandbox as an ordinary environment variable
options.says: Ruled out because for production agents, "keep the value out of the sandbox".

options.text: Log the value once at the start so later checks can compare it
options.says: Ruled out because "A key that appears in a tool result or an audit line has left your control."

options.text: Keep the value out of the model's reach, and redact it in logs
options.says: The page says "a secret never enters anything the model can read or a file anyone can commit", and "In logs and results, redact before writing."

origin.section: Secrets in development and in production
